clue.text: Modified missile they compare (not literally)

indicators.note: To modify a thing is to alter what it is made of, and letters altered are letters no longer standing in the order they were handed over in.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a line from an arms report, and the joke is that a weapon gets turned into a figure of speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A simile likens one thing to another with 'like' or 'as', so it compares without ever claiming the two things really are the same.

clue.text: Bias added to a line in personal kind of column

parts.note: spin is the bias a press officer puts on a story
the word a, taken exactly as it stands
l is the usual abbreviation for line, as on a map or in a script

explanation.walkthrough: Three kinds of column are in play at once: the newspaper sort the surface is hinting at, the architectural sort, and the one every person carries about inside them.
explanation.definitionFit: The column meant is anatomical — the backbone — so 'personal' is doing real work, marking it off from a building's column or a newspaper's.

clue.text: Waist hit when batting — precisely

definitions.meaning: the part of the body a belt goes round
a cricketer who strikes the ball off the dead centre of the bat has done this to it

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a batter taking a blow on the body, which lets two unrelated senses sit in one sentence: one anatomical, one straight off the bat.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's middle is their waist, and in cricket to middle a ball is to strike it dead centre of the bat — the precise version of a hit.

clue.text: Heard you and I ruled tax out of order, had it very easy

indicators.note: Something out of order is not in its proper sequence, so the letters it labels have to be resequenced.
It asks for the sound of the words rather than their spelling, and two pronouns spoken out are single letters when written down.

parts.note: said aloud, the letters U and I are exactly those two pronouns
anagram fodder, eight letters, joined by the two letters heard above

explanation.walkthrough: 'Heard' is doing the work that makes the sums add up: eight letters of fodder plus the two you can only get by saying the pronouns aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: To luxuriate is to wallow in comfort and take your time over it, which is what having it very easy looks like from the outside.

clue.text: Tool that's sharp but may be said to be blunt

definitions.text: Tool that's sharp but may be said to be blunt

parts.note: the surface promises a digging implement with a keen edge, and that much is plainly true of the thing

parts.words: may be said to be blunt
parts.note: 'said' is the hinge — there is a stock phrase about naming a thing by its plainest name, and using it is what counts as speaking bluntly

explanation.walkthrough: A card suit runs right through this puzzle, and the pointed black symbol on the cards is sharp in a second way the clue never quite admits to.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue describes one object twice: the edged garden implement, and the word a plain speaker is proverbially told to use for what it is.

clue.text: For Americans, field that's extremely hard

definitions.meaning: the baseball infield, named for the shape the four bases mark out
the hardest natural substance there is, right at the top of the mineral scale

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are straight definitions, one geographic and one material, and the only misdirection is letting 'hard' sound like a remark about the field.
explanation.definitionFit: American baseball calls its infield the diamond, and the gem is the hardest natural substance known, so the second half names it by its defining property.

clue.text: Firing careless shot might result in this

definitions.meaning: the formal word for being let go from a job

definitions.text: careless shot might result in this
definitions.meaning: in cricket a rash stroke gets a batter out, and this is how the scorecard records it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Firing' and 'shot' both pull the surface towards a gun, and neither sense of the answer has anything to do with one — the second belongs to cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Losing a job is a firing; in cricket a batter losing their wicket to a rash stroke is recorded under the very same word.

clue.text: Perfectly performed in most social classes

indicators.note: It means all but one of a group, the group being the lettered scale people are graded on — though it stays vague about which one is left behind.

parts.note: Britain's social grades are lettered A, B, C, D and E, and four of those five letters are what get strung together

explanation.walkthrough: Social grade is one of the crossword's quieter conventions — A to E, straight off a market researcher's form — and here it supplies every letter of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To ace something is to carry it off flawlessly, a tennis serve or an exam, so in the past tense it covers any performance done without a fault.

clue.text: Covered as a learner, I drove erratically

indicators.note: Doing a thing erratically is doing it to no settled pattern, so the letters come out in no reliable sequence.

parts.note: a stays as it is, and a learner driver shows an L plate
the remaining six letters of the fodder

explanation.walkthrough: The L-plate is the piece to spot: 'learner' is one of the reliable single-letter conventions, hiding here inside a sentence that is entirely about driving.
explanation.definitionFit: To overlay is to lay one thing over another so the lower one stops showing, which is what covering does — the definition matches the past participle.

clue.text: A coach secured by side in disarray? Correct

indicators.note: To be secured by something is to be held fast inside it, so the pieces named first finish up enclosed.

parts.note: the four letters of SIDE shaken up, then opened out to make room

indicators.note: Disarray is the state of things knocked out of their proper places, which is what happens to these four letters.

parts.note: the first word of the clue, used as itself
a coach is a bus — the vehicle, not the trainer the surface offers

explanation.walkthrough: 'Correct' is a verb here, the sort you do to a person rather than to a proof, and 'coach' is the pivot the whole sporting surface turns on.
explanation.definitionFit: To disabuse someone is to put them right about something they wrongly believe, so 'Correct' is the verb sense — to set straight, not to be accurate.

clue.text: Last part of book, perhaps, some find exciting

indicators.note: 'Some' of a phrase is a portion of it, and the portion wanted is a run of consecutive letters rather than a piece of the meaning.

parts.note: five letters in a row bridge the gap between these two words

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing in the surface suggests concealment except 'some', which is carrying a whole instruction while looking like ordinary vagueness.
explanation.definitionFit: An index sits at the back of a reference book; 'perhaps' concedes that plenty of books finish with something else, so this is one example of a last part.

clue.text: Respondents, as can be seen, covering all points about right

indicators.note: To cover a thing is to lie over it from both sides, so the word doing the covering parts and the rest settles between its halves.

parts.note: the word AS used exactly as printed, then parted
the four points of the compass, N, S, W and E
re heads a memo and means about, concerning
r is the usual abbreviation for right

explanation.walkthrough: Compass points are a standard supply of letters and 'all points' asks for the whole set; the order they come out in is fixed by what has to be spelled.
explanation.definitionFit: A respondent is someone who answers — a survey, a question, a petition — so the definition is the formal register of the same plural noun.

clue.text: Recalling upset about drug producing bad reaction

indicators.note: Upsetting a thing tips its contents out, and they land in no particular arrangement.
It puts the extra letter in among the others rather than tacking it on at either end.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters
E is the tabloid shorthand for ecstasy, one letter joined to the fodder

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a memory that provokes somebody, which is very nearly the shape of the definition — but the reaction wanted here is a medical one.
explanation.definitionFit: Something allergenic brings on an allergic response, a bad reaction in the strict clinical sense rather than merely an unpopular one.

clue.text: Arsenal's example of this weapon

definitions.meaning: the north London football side is one instance of the sporting sense
a heavy stick, the oldest weapon of the lot

explanation.walkthrough: An arsenal is a weapons store, so the sentence holds together perfectly — while the name it is really pointing at belongs to a football ground in north London.
explanation.definitionFit: A club is a heavy stick swung as a weapon, and the side named in the clue is one instance of the other sense, a sporting association.

clue.text: It takes several horses to move it inches?

definitions.text: It takes several horses to move it inches?

parts.words: It takes several horses to move it
parts.note: the surface offers something too heavy to shift; the setter means a carriage pulled by a team, and the enumeration counts the team
horses are measured in hands, and the question is how many inches make one of those units — read as a plain sentence, the answer replies

explanation.walkthrough: Read as an ordinary phrase the answer is arithmetic, so many inches to a hand; read as a noun it is a carriage and its team. The clue wants both at once.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a team of horses harnessed to one vehicle and, taken literally, the number of inches that make up a hand.

clue.text: They help thieves steal handbags etc.

definitions.meaning: in law, people who assist a crime without carrying it out themselves
the bags, belts and scarves that finish an outfit off

explanation.walkthrough: One word, two worlds — the criminal courts and the fashion pages — and the clue lays them end to end so that the join disappears.
explanation.definitionFit: In law an accessory assists a crime without committing it; in a wardrobe the same word covers the bags and belts that finish an outfit.

clue.text: Complicity in conflict, having change of heart

indicators.note: A word's heart is the letter at its dead centre, and changing it means swapping that single letter for another.

parts.note: a conflict between two things is a collision
the fifth of those nine letters steps aside and U takes the vacant place

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a peace-talks headline, where a change of heart would be a change of mind; here it is strictly the letter sitting in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Collusion is secret cooperation towards a dishonest end, and complicity is that same involvement seen from the side of blame.

clue.text: Being promoted on board — for French, that upset good number

parts.note: the French word for 'that'

indicators.note: Upset is turned over, and in a down entry that means the letters are read back up the column.

parts.note: g is the standard abbreviation for good, as on a school report
the number is left unnamed, and the count of letters still to fill settles which one it is

explanation.walkthrough: 'On board' is the chessboard: a pawn reaching the far rank is promoted, and the piece almost everyone chooses gives the manoeuvre its name.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess a pawn that reaches the far rank is promoted, and the standard choice of piece is what the process is named after.

clue.text: Faction supporting gang in area close to fighting

indicators.note: What supports a thing stands underneath it, and underneath in a down entry means later in the answer.

parts.note: a ring is an organised gang — a drugs ring, a betting ring
a side is a faction in a dispute

explanation.walkthrough: Boxing is nowhere in the surface, which is all street gangs, and the ring that supplies the first half is a criminal one rather than the roped kind.
explanation.definitionFit: The seats nearest a boxing ring are the ringside ones, so the definition describes the spot literally rather than offering a synonym.

clue.text: Like life as simple as possible? I'll run a clue that's convoluted

definitions.text: Like life as simple as possible?

indicators.note: Something convoluted is twisted round on itself, and letters twisted round each other stop reading in the order given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

explanation.walkthrough: The setter's aside about writing a twisty clue is the clue's own raw material, which is the joke: the fodder describes what is being done to it.
explanation.definitionFit: A unicellular organism is a single cell, the least complicated thing that counts as alive, so the definition points at the simplest form life takes.

clue.text: Short rhyme for it will, when spoken quickly

indicators.note: It asks only for a word that chimes with what follows, not one that matches it throughout, so just the ending is handed over.
Said at speed the two words before it collapse into one contracted sound, and that sound is what has to be matched.

parts.note: run together in speech those two words become a single contraction, and the answer is the word that chimes with it

explanation.walkthrough: This is a rhyme rather than a strict soundalike: the clue hands over the ending and leaves you to supply the letter that starts the word off.
explanation.definitionFit: Short and little are everyday synonyms for small extent, though short tends to measure length and little size — that overlap is what the setter uses.

clue.text: Emoji used by wooer in suit

definitions.meaning: the red symbol a suitor sends by text

definitions.note: The answer is a plural noun that names one single suit of cards, which is why the singular 'suit' defines it fairly.
definitions.meaning: one of the two red suits in a pack of cards

explanation.walkthrough: The suit and the emoji are the same picture, which is the whole point: a romantic text and a hand of cards get by on one symbol between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearts is one of the four suits in a pack, and the red heart is the standard emoji of romantic intent — one shape doing two jobs.

clue.text: Soccer goalkeeper goofed thus (once in each half)

indicators.note: It promises the letters lie buried in a run, and that the run turns up twice — one instance on either side of the sentence.

parts.note: four consecutive letters bridge the end of one word and the start of the next
the same four letters run again across the join before this word, which is what makes the bracketed promise true

explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed aside reads as a match report — a goal let in during each half — and it is really telling you the letters are there twice over.
explanation.definitionFit: Ergo is the Latin for 'therefore', kept alive in English for drawing a conclusion, which is exactly the job 'thus' does.

clue.text: Volume in English about an isolated regime

indicators.note: Set around a thing, it tells you the measure just named opens up and the next word settles inside it.

parts.note: a quart is a measure of volume, two pints of it
the word an, lifted straight out of the clue
the word in, also used as itself
E is the standard abbreviation for English

explanation.walkthrough: 'Volume' looks like a book, especially standing next to 'English', and it is a liquid measure instead — the swap that makes an unrelated set of pieces read smoothly.
explanation.definitionFit: A quarantine is the enforced routine of keeping the possibly infected apart, so 'regime' here means an imposed regimen rather than a government.

clue.text: Once more restrict speech, for example in newspaper

indicators.note: The little word marks an insertion: whatever comes before it drops inside whatever comes after.

parts.note: a rag is a slighting word for a newspaper, and it opens between its first and second letters
e.g. is the everyday shorthand for 'for example'

explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs to four words before any wordplay starts, so the sentence about jokes in the press is doing nothing but hiding two short pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Gagging is stopping a mouth, so this is that silencing applied a second time — 'once more' is carried by the prefix in front.

clue.text: Device for lifting injured hill-climber

definitions.meaning: the screw device that raises a car off the ground to change a wheel
the boy of the nursery rhyme who fell down and broke his crown

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is a person rather than a thing: the nursery rhyme supplies the name, and the tumble down the slope supplies the injury.
explanation.definitionFit: A jack raises a car off the road, and the boy of the rhyme who went up the hill and broke his crown carries the same name.

clue.text: Following one action of union, embracing it

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: To embrace a thing is to put your arms right round it, so the word before closes over the word after.

parts.note: union in the biological sense, and the act of it
the word it, dropped in whole

explanation.walkthrough: 'Union' reads like a trade union standing next to 'action', and that is the misdirection — the union wanted is the biological one.
explanation.definitionFit: To imitate someone is to follow their example, so 'Following' is meant in the sense of taking after rather than walking behind.

clue.text: Succeeding with a more stern position?

parts.note: aft is the position towards a ship's stern
the ending that makes an adjective comparative, as in 'sterner'

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a nautical joke: at sea this really is a comparative, meaning further towards the stern of the ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean coming next in sequence — the succeeding day and the day it follows are one and the same day.

clue.text: Last of aging female's family that may be prepared to help in a pickle

definitions.text: may be prepared to help in a pickle

indicators.note: It takes the final letter of the word behind it and nothing else, which is how a seven-letter answer can begin from a single one.

parts.note: the final letter of aginG
what belongs to a female is hers, three letters of possessive
kin is family, in the collective sense

explanation.walkthrough: 'In a pickle' is the idiom for being in trouble, and the definition takes it at face value instead — what goes into the jar.
explanation.definitionFit: A gherkin is a small cucumber preserved in vinegar, so the definition describes it by what is done to it and where it ends up.

clue.text: Beautiful woman performs without love in theatre part

indicators.note: Here it means lacking rather than outside, so the letter named after it is taken away from the word in front.

parts.note: the gods are the highest and cheapest gallery in a theatre

indicators.note: It marks the insertion: what has just been assembled goes inside the thing named next.

parts.note: performs in the sense of does — she does a fine job
love is a score of nothing at tennis, written as a nought, and it is the letter that leaves

explanation.walkthrough: 'Theatre part' looks like a role and turns out to be a place in the building — the gallery up under the roof that everybody calls the gods.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling a woman a goddess is settled English hyperbole for striking beauty, a figurative sense the dictionaries record beside the literal deity.
